options.text: A continuous tube from mouth to anus through which food passes
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
The canal includes mouth and oesophagus too.

options.text: The organs that make digestive juices
options.explanation: Those are the accessory organs, not the canal.

options.text: The blood vessels serving the gut
options.explanation: Vessels are not part of the tube.

questions.stem: Which region carries out most digestion and absorption?

options.explanation: It transports food by peristalsis.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The stomach churns and acidifies; absorption is limited there.
It absorbs water from the residue.

questions.stem: Which of these is an accessory structure rather than part of the canal?

options.explanation: It is the central canal segment.
Ingestion starts the canal.
Correct — this matches the account taught above.
The stomach is a canal region.

questions.stem: What is the main role of the large intestine?

options.explanation: Protein digestion happens earlier.
Bile does that in the small intestine.
The gall bladder stores bile.

options.text: Absorbing the remaining water from the undigested residue
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

questions.stem: Why is the pancreas described as accessory?

options.text: Food does not pass through it, but its secretions serve digestion
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Because it is smaller than the stomach
options.explanation: Size is not the criterion.
It secretes whenever chyme arrives.
Absorption is the intestine's job.

questions.stem: List the canal's regions in order from mouth onwards.
questions.modelAnswer: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, then large intestine.

questions.stem: Name two accessory organs of digestion.
questions.modelAnswer: The liver and the pancreas — or the gall bladder — aid digestion as accessory organs.

questions.stem: Explain why the canal needs regional specialisation at all.
questions.modelAnswer: Because ingestion, transport, acid churning, enzymatic digestion, absorption and water recovery need different conditions and structures; one uniform tube could not provide the acidity of the stomach and the alkalinity of the intestine at the same time.

questions.stem: A swallowed bolus reaches the stomach. Trace its route to the blood, naming each canal region en route.
questions.modelAnswer: From the stomach it is churned into chyme, passes into the small intestine where enzymes digest it and villi absorb the soluble products into the blood, while the residue continues to the large intestine for water recovery.
